NoteImport of the original report

Report dated October 15, 2026, imported into the blog on November 5, 2026 with static outputs and no analysis rerun. This educational study uses synthetic video data: its hypotheses and recommendations describe the experiment and do not establish effects on a real platform. Original figure labels, code comments and literal strings remain unchanged, including Portuguese text inside code; numerical formatting is also preserved. The source contains discrepancies between its narrative and some tables; the values remain unchanged for traceability.

Business context and hypotheses

Allocating editorial budgets and designing recommendation systems for video platforms require separating the inertia of a channel’s accumulated audience from content factors under the creator’s control. In the audited dataset of 12.00012.000 videos across 1515 editorial categories (viral_videos.csv), the binary virality indicator (viral = 1) is deterministically defined by the 8080th percentile (P80P_{80}) of view counts (views), with an exact boundary between 734.299734.299 and 734.379734.379 views (2.4002.400 viral videos and a base rate of 20,00%20,00\%).

Executive summary of the experiment

  1. Structural dominance of the subscriber base (H1H_1 supported): The logarithmic subscriber count (ln⁡(1+subscriber_count)\ln(1 + \text{subscriber\_count})) has a correlation of r=0,8097r = 0,8097 (p<10−300p < 10^{-300}) with ln⁡(1+views)\ln(1 + \text{views}) and alone explains 65,56%65,56\% of total variance (R2=0,6556R^2 = 0,6556). In the pre-publication LightGBM model, channel size accounts for 93,59%93,59\% of total information gain in regression and 80,09%80,09\% in classification.
  2. Simpson’s paradox in video duration (H2H_2 supported): The negative marginal correlation between duration_sec and ln⁡(1+views)\ln(1 + \text{views}) (r=−0,2015,p=3,97×10−110r = -0,2015, p = 3,97 \times 10^{-110}) arises from category confounding. Short-video categories (Music, with a median of 239s239\text{s} and 57,2%57,2\% virality; Comedy, with 297s297\text{s} and 35,2%35,2\%) contain channels 5x5\text{x} to 10x10\text{x} larger than long-video categories (Travel, Vlog). After normalizing by channel size (ln⁡(views/subscriber_count)\ln(\text{views}/\text{subscriber\_count})), the duration effect disappears (r=−0,0077,p=0,3966r = -0,0077, p = 0,3966).
  3. Actionable creator factors in the simulation (H3H_3 supported): Including a human face in the thumbnail (thumbnail_face = 1) raises the virality rate from 18,15%18,15\% to 22,78%22,78\%, a relative increase of +25,52%+25,52\% (p=9,34×10−32p = 9,34 \times 10^{-32}), and increases the views-per-subscriber ratio by +24,39%+24,39\%. Indexing density through tags_count retains a positive correlation after adjustment for confounding (r=+0,0549,p=1,83×10−9r = +0,0549, p = 1,83 \times 10^{-9}).
  4. Upload date and time neutrality (H4H_4 supported): Publication hour (upload_hour, Kruskal-Wallis p=0,6606p = 0,6606) and day of the week (upload_day, Kruskal-Wallis p=0,8717p = 0,8717) show no statistically significant effect on relative reach in this dataset.
  5. Sufficiency of the pre-publication regime (H5H_5 supported): Adding six relative post-upload engagement rates (Regime B) changes the test PR-AUC by only +0,0051+0,0051 in LightGBM (0,7185→0,72370,7185 \to 0,7237) and leaves regression performance unchanged (RMSLE of 0,95840,9584 versus 0,95780,9578, p=0,8331p = 0,8331). The regularized linear model (LogisticRegression / Ridge) and dual convergence of the LGBMRegressor thresholded at quantile P80P_{80} achieve PR-AUC of 0,73830,7383 to 0,74090,7409 and ROC-AUC of 0,90720,9072 to 0,90940,9094 at upload time (cold start).

Central problem and audience skewness

Modeling digital attention metrics on their original scale produces unstable estimators. Raw view counts (views) range from 347347 to 158.516.795158.516.795, with a mean of 1.000.6421.000.642, median of 179.680179.680, positive skewness of +29,532+29,532 and excess kurtosis of 1.305,181.305,18. A single extreme observation in the right tail dominates ordinary squared loss.

Stabilization through the natural logarithmic transformation yreg=ln⁡(1+views)y_{\text{reg}} = \ln(1 + \text{views}) corrects this structural distortion. On the logarithmic scale, the distribution approaches a well-behaved Gaussian with a mean of 12,08912,089, standard deviation of 1,6361,636, skewness of +0,053+0,053 and excess kurtosis of +0,080+0,080. The subscriber base (subscriber_count) follows the same pattern: its skewness falls from +14,472+14,472 on the raw scale to +0,145+0,145 under ln⁡(1+subscriber_count)\ln(1 + \text{subscriber\_count}).

Falsifiable hypotheses (H1H_1 to H5H_5) and mathematical rationale for the metrics

The study follows five falsifiable hypotheses formulated before estimating the supervised models:

  • H1H_1 (Subscriber-base dominance): Logarithmic channel size alone accounts for more than 60%60\% of the variance of ln⁡(1+views)\ln(1 + \text{views}) and more than 75%75\% of information gain in tree-based models.
  • H2H_2 (Simpson’s paradox in duration): The apparent negative correlation between duration_sec and views (r<−0,18r < -0,18) results from confounding between editorial category and channel size, becoming negligible (|r|<0,02,p>0,05|r| < 0,02, p > 0,05) when evaluated against the multiplier ln⁡(views/subscriber_count)\ln(\text{views}/\text{subscriber\_count}).
  • H3H_3 (Creator packaging factors): thumbnail_face and tags_count retain a positive, statistically significant effect (p<0,001p < 0,001) after removing the effect of subscriber_count.
  • H4H_4 (Scheduling neutrality): upload_hour and upload_day have no significant effect (p>0,05p > 0,05) on view counts or the virality rate.
  • H5H_5 (Practical equivalence between cold start and relative post-upload signals): Adding relative engagement rates (likes/views, comments/views, shares/views) produces a marginal predictive gain below 0,0150,015 in PR-AUC and RMSLE compared with the model restricted to pre-upload metadata.

To respect the lognormal geometry of view counts and the minority prevalence of the positive class (20,0%20,0\%), the study uses two complementary metric families:

  1. Continuous regression (y=ln⁡(1+views)y = \ln(1 + \text{views})): The primary metric is RMSLE (Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error), accompanied by MAEln\text{MAE}_{\ln}, Rln⁡2R^2_{\ln} and MdAPE (Median Absolute Percentage Error on the original view-count scale). Because 𝔼[exp⁡(y)]≠exp⁡(𝔼[y])\mathbb{E}[\exp(y)] \neq \exp(\mathbb{E}[y]) under logarithmic residuals with finite variance, retransformation to count space applies the nonparametric smearing estimator from Duan, 1983:

V̂i=max⁡(0,ŝDuan⋅exp(ŷi)−1),where ŝDuan=1Ntr∑j=1Ntrexp⁡(yj−ŷj)\hat{V}_i = \max\left(0,\; \hat{s}_{\text{Duan}} \cdot \exp(\hat{y}_i) - 1\right), \quad \text{where } \hat{s}_{\text{Duan}} = \frac{1}{N_{\text{tr}}} \sum_{j=1}^{N_{\text{tr}}} \exp\left(y_j - \hat{y}_j\right)

  1. Calibrated binary classification (ybin=𝕀[views≥734.379]y_{\text{bin}} = \mathbb{I}[\text{views} \ge 734.379]): The primary ranking metric is the area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC / Average Precision), whose random reference value equals the base rate π=0,2000\pi = 0,2000. The study also evaluates ROC-AUC, Brier Score (probability calibration) and F1@P80 (F1 evaluated at threshold τ80\tau_{80}, corresponding to the 8080th percentile of training-estimated probabilities and aligning the 20%20\% selection rate with the target’s structural definition).

Data audit and quality contracts

The module src/youtube_viral/contracts.py programmatically enforces the integrity of the raw data and feature matrices. No transformation or hyperparameter tuning occurs before the seven formal contracts (DC-01 to DC-07) pass.

Volume, types and logarithmic stabilization (log1p)

The following cell loads the pipeline’s audited artifacts and summarizes the distributional properties of numeric variables on their original scale and after logarithmic transformation.

import json
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

df_raw = pd.read_csv("viral_videos.csv")
with open("reports/metrics/summary_results.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    summary = json.load(f)

audit_rows = []
for col, apply_log in [
    ("views", False),
    ("views", True),
    ("subscriber_count", False),
    ("subscriber_count", True),
    ("duration_sec", False),
    ("title_length", False),
    ("tags_count", False),
    ("description_length", False),
]:
    vals = df_raw[col].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    label = f"ln(1 + {col})" if apply_log else col
    if apply_log:
        vals = np.log1p(vals)
    audit_rows.append(
        {
            "Variável": label,
            "Média": round(float(np.mean(vals)), 3),
            "Desvio Padrão": round(float(np.std(vals)), 3),
            "Mediana (P50)": round(float(np.median(vals)), 3),
            "P80": round(float(np.percentile(vals, 80)), 3),
            "Skewness": round(float(stats.skew(vals)), 3),
            "Kurtosis": round(float(stats.kurtosis(vals)), 3),
        }
    )

pd.DataFrame(audit_rows)

The records are complete: zero null cells, 12.00012.000 unique identifiers (vid_000001 to vid_012000) and all 1515 editorial categories populated with between 745745 (Food) and 844844 (Finance) videos.

Target and proxy leakage diagnostics (P80P_{80} and post-upload signals)

The statistical audit identified two information-leakage vectors that would invalidate a naive model using every column in the CSV file:

  1. Deterministic target leakage (views ↔\leftrightarrow viral): The maximum view count among nonviral videos is 734.299734.299, while the minimum among viral videos is 734.379734.379. Because viral is an exact step function of views at quantile P80P_{80}, retaining views (or any monotonic transformation of views) in the classification predictor matrix XX produces artificial 100%100\% separation.
  2. Proxy leakage in absolute engagement counts (likes, comments, shares): The dataset’s generation process simulated interactions by multiplying views by category-specific rates. Consequently, raw counts have logarithmic correlations of r=0,9736r = 0,9736 (likes), r=0,9601r = 0,9601 (comments) and r=0,9495r = 0,9495 (shares) with ln⁡(1+views)\ln(1 + \text{views}). Including raw engagement counts in XX gives the model a noisy copy of the response variable. In contrast, view-normalized rates (like_rate, comment_rate, share_rate) have virtually zero correlation with ln⁡(1+views)\ln(1 + \text{views}) (r∈[−0,0171;−0,0004]r \in [-0,0171;\, -0,0004]), separating qualitative engagement from the raw scale of reach.

Runtime validation contracts (DC-01 to DC-07)

The module contracts.py runs seven formal guards before feature generation and before training each estimator:

Code Contract rule Audited empirical check
DC-01 Volume and primary-key uniqueness Exactly 12.00012.000 rows, 1515 columns and 12.00012.000 distinct video_id values.
DC-02 Strict completeness 00 null values (NaN/None) across all 1515 columns.
DC-03 Closed domain of categorical variables 1515 editorial categories and 77 days of the week (Mon to Sun).
DC-04 Physical bounds of pre-upload metadata duration_sec ∈[30,7184]\in [30, 7184], title_length ∈[10,100]\in [10, 100], upload_hour ∈[0,23]\in [0, 23], tags_count ∈[0,30]\in [0, 30], description_length ∈[0,2000]\in [0, 2000].
DC-05 Engagement and size consistency subscriber_count ≥100\ge 100, views ≥1\ge 1, likes ≤\le views, comments ≤\le views and shares ≤\le views.
DC-06 Integrity of the target’s P80P_{80} boundary Rate of viral == 1 equal to 20,00%20,00\% and max⁡(views∣viral=0)<min⁡(views∣viral=1)\max(\text{views} \mid \text{viral}=0) < \min(\text{views} \mid \text{viral}=1).
DC-07 Regime-specific leakage guard Prohibits views, viral, likes, comments and shares in XX globally; blocks post-upload rates in Regime A.

Exploratory analysis and feature engineering

Following the principles of visual clarity and reduced cognitive load, the study’s five figures use aligned double panels (1x2, figsize=(12, 5.2), dpi=300, square box aspect ratio set_box_aspect(1)), connecting each business question to its statistical evidence.

Lognormal distributions and deterministic virality boundary (Figure 1)

Figure 1 documents the transition from the original long tail to logarithmic normality in Panel (a), and shows the coupling between channel size, view counts and the deterministic virality boundary (ln⁡(1+734.379)≈13,507\ln(1 + 734.379) \approx 13,507) in Panel (b).

Panel (b) supports Hypothesis H1H_1 within the simulation: the steep positive slope reflects the correlation of r=0,8097r = 0,8097 between ln⁡(1+subscriber_count)\ln(1 + \text{subscriber\_count}) and ln⁡(1+views)\ln(1 + \text{views}). Channels with more than 1 million1\text{ million} subscribers (ln⁡(1+subs)>13,8\ln(1 + \text{subs}) > 13,8) cross the horizontal line at 734.379734.379 views even when their videos perform below their own audience’s average in relative terms.

Decomposing Simpson’s paradox across categories and duration (Figure 2)

A superficial inspection would suggest that longer videos reduce reach (r=−0,2015,p=3,97×10−110r = -0,2015, p = 3,97 \times 10^{-110}). Figure 2 decomposes this phenomenon across the 1515 editorial categories.

Panel (a) reveals the confounding structure: Music (57,2%57,2\% viral videos) and Comedy (35,2%35,2\%) have large median subscriber counts (2,06 million2,06\text{ million} and 850 thousand850\text{ thousand}) and short durations (239s239\text{s} and 297s297\text{s}). At the opposite end, Vlog, Food, DIY, Lifestyle and Travel have virality rates between 6,6%6,6\% and 9,4%9,4\% because their channels have median subscriber counts of 190 thousand190\text{ thousand} to 220 thousand220\text{ thousand}. When Panel (b) controls for the channel effect through standardized scores (Z-scores), the raw slope of r=−0,2015r = -0,2015 collapses to a horizontal line (r=−0,0077,p=0,3966r = -0,0077, p = 0,3966). In this simulated dataset, video duration neither reduces nor increases organic reach per subscriber.

Actionable creator factors and scheduling neutrality (Figure 3)

After adjusting for channel-size confounding, Figure 3 isolates the factors creators can control before publication.

Panel (a) supports Hypothesis H3H_3. Although channels using faces in thumbnails (thumbnail_face = 1, 40,0%40,0\% of the dataset) have the same median size as the others (≈381k\approx 381\text{k} subscribers), their virality rate rises from 18,15%18,15\% to 22,78%22,78\% (+25,52%+25,52\% relative; Welch’s tt test t=12,24,p=3,47×10−34t = 12,24, p = 3,47 \times 10^{-34}; Mann-Whitney p=9,34×10−32p = 9,34 \times 10^{-32}). The density distribution of tags_count also grows monotonically, raising the mean multiplier ln⁡(views/subs)\ln(\text{views}/\text{subs}) from −0,78-0,78 (0 to 5 tags) to −0,66-0,66 (21 to 30 tags; r=+0,0549,p=1,83×10−9r = +0,0549, p = 1,83 \times 10^{-9}).

Panel (b) supports Hypothesis H4H_4: across the 2424 hours of the day, the virality rate fluctuates within the sampling-variation band around 20,0%20,0\% (χ2=25,76,p=0,3121\chi^2 = 25,76, p = 0,3121), and the logarithmic multiplier remains flat (Kruskal-Wallis H=19,69,p=0,6606H = 19,69, p = 0,6606). The day of the week shows the same null pattern (Kruskal-Wallis H=2,47,p=0,8717H = 2,47, p = 0,8717).

Feature-regime specification (Regime A cold start versus Regime B relative signals)

To formally test Hypothesis H5H_5 without proxy leakage, the module src/youtube_viral/features.py builds two strictly separated feature matrices:

  • Regime A (Cold Start / Pre-publication, 18 features): Contains the 99 original features available before upload (category, subscriber_count, duration_sec, title_length, thumbnail_face, upload_hour, upload_day, tags_count, description_length) plus 99 deterministic domain transformations: log_subscriber_count (ln⁡(1+subs)\ln(1+\text{subs})), log_duration_sec (ln⁡(1+duration_sec)\ln(1+\text{duration\_sec})), tags_per_title_char, desc_to_title_ratio, cyclic hour encoding (hour_sin, hour_cos), the is_weekend indicator (Sat/Sun) and the has_tags and has_description flags.
  • Regime B (Relative Post-upload Early Signals, 24 features): Extends Regime A with 66 dimensionless engagement ratios: like_rate (likes/views\text{likes}/\text{views}), comment_rate (comments/views\text{comments}/\text{views}), share_rate (shares/views\text{shares}/\text{views}), engagement_rate_total ((likes+comments+shares)/views(\text{likes}+\text{comments}+\text{shares})/\text{views}), comments_per_like and shares_per_like. Contract DC-07 continues to block all raw counts.

Statistical modeling and machine learning

Stratified split protocol (80/20) and 5-fold cross-validation

The dataset of 12.00012.000 videos was deterministically partitioned (SEED = 42) into Training (Ntr=9.600N_{\text{tr}} = 9.600, 80%80\%) and Holdout test (Nte=2.400N_{\text{te}} = 2.400, 20%20\%) sets, using joint stratification by the composite key category + "_" + viral (3030 strata). The original report states that this design preserves the 20,00%20,00\% proportion of viral videos and the balance among the 1515 categories in both partitions, with internal cross-validation conducted over 55 stratified folds of the training set.

Three-part architecture: logarithmic regression, calibrated classification and confounding adjustment

The implementation in src/youtube_viral/modeling.py contains three complementary estimation tasks:

  1. Task 1 (Logarithmic regression of ln⁡(1+views)\ln(1 + \text{views})): Compares a category-stratified baseline estimator (predicting the category’s historical mean of ln⁡(1+views)\ln(1 + \text{views}) within the training fold) against Ridge (α=1,0\alpha = 1,0 with StandardScaler and OneHotEncoder), RandomForestRegressor (300300 trees, max_depth=12) and LGBMRegressor (300300 trees, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=31, subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8).
  2. Task 2 (Calibrated binary classification and dual convergence at P80P_{80}): Compares the empirical category baseline against LogisticRegression (L2L_2, C=1,0C=1,0), RandomForestClassifier, LGBMClassifier and the hybrid estimator LightGBM_DualRegressor, which uses the LightGBM regressor’s continuous prediction ŷreg\hat{y}_{\text{reg}} to rank virality probability (through univariate logistic calibration) and applies the exact 8080th-percentile threshold (τ80\tau_{80}).
  3. Task 3 (Confounding-adjusted organic-efficiency model): Trains a LGBMRegressor directly on the logarithmic multiplier M=ln⁡(views/subscriber_count)M = \ln(\text{views}/\text{subscriber\_count}), removing subscriber_count and log_subscriber_count from XX to isolate the contribution of content metadata.

Why does dual convergence (LightGBM_DualRegressor) outperform the direct classifier in this experiment?

When LGBMClassifier trains directly on the binary viral label, a video with 730.000730.000 views (viral = 0) receives exactly the same nominal loss as a video with 500500 views (viral = 0), discarding information about distance to the 734.379734.379 boundary. LightGBM_DualRegressor preserves the full metric resolution of ln⁡(1+views)\ln(1 + \text{views}) while fitting the trees and discretizes only at the decision stage (ŷ≥τ80=13,2225\hat{y} \ge \tau_{80} = 13,2225). On the Regime A test set, PR-AUC rises from 0,71850,7185 to 0,73830,7383 (+0,0198+0,0198) and F1@P80 from 0,64930,6493 to 0,66390,6639, approaching the leading parametric model’s performance (LogisticRegression, PR-AUC = 0,7407 and F1@P80 = 0,6701).

Evaluation, diagnostics and explainability

Precision-recall curves and continuous calibration on the test set (Figure 4)

Figure 4 shows the performance of the pre-publication models (Regime A) on the holdout test set (N=2.400N = 2.400, including 481481 viral videos).

In Panel (a), all supervised curves maintain precision above 85%85\% up to 40%40\% recall and converge at the F1@P80 operating point, with balanced precision and recall of 66,5%–67,1%66,5\%\text{--}67,1\% (versus 36,0%36,0\% precision for the category baseline). In Panel (b), the continuous LGBMRegressor predictions follow the perfect-calibration diagonal y=ŷy = \hat{y} across five orders of magnitude, and the horizontal dashed line (τ80=13,22\tau_{80} = 13,22) separates the upper-right quadrant of viral videos.

Formal comparison of Regime A versus Regime B and gain/SHAP explainability (Figure 5)

To audit LightGBM internally without tree-cardinality distortions, the study extracts both percentage loss-reduction gain (importance_type="gain") and exact TreeSHAP marginal contributions (Lundberg & Lee, 2017) on the test set. Figure 5 summarizes the explainability ranking in Regime A and its direct contrast with Regime B.

The exact numbers exported by the pipeline document the problem’s structure visually and analytically:

Reading Figure 5 and Table 4 together clarifies two central mechanisms:

  1. Absolute-volume hierarchy (Regime A): subscriber_count (66,89%66,89\% of gain; |SHAP|=0,7774|\text{SHAP}| = 0,7774) and log_subscriber_count (26,70%26,70\% of gain; |SHAP|=0,2575|\text{SHAP}| = 0,2575) account for 93,59%93,59\% of the total reduction in logarithmic squared error. Among content metadata, the leading features are category (1,21%1,21\%), tags_per_title_char (0,73%0,73\%) and thumbnail_face (0,71%0,71\% of split gain, but the 3rd-largest local TreeSHAP impact, with |SHAP|=0,0972|\text{SHAP}| = 0,0972, exceeding category in per-video impact).
  2. Confounding-adjusted hierarchy (ln⁡(views/subscriber_count)\ln(\text{views}/\text{subscriber\_count})) and post-upload signals (Regime B): Removing the subscriber base in Task 3 brings content features to the foreground in the following gain ranking: category (16,58%16,58\%), thumbnail_face (14,62%14,62\%, largest |SHAP||\text{SHAP}| at 0,09550,0955), desc_to_title_ratio (10,30%10,30\%), title_length (9,85%9,85\%), description_length (8,68%8,68\%) and tags_count (8,04%8,04\%, 2nd-largest |SHAP||\text{SHAP}| at 0,03210,0321). In Regime B, all 66 engagement-rate variables combined (shares_per_like, comment_rate, comments_per_like, share_rate, like_rate, engagement_rate_total) account for only 2,47%2,47\% of total regression gain and 9,08%9,08\% of classification gain. The resulting net test improvement is statistically indistinguishable in regression (ΔRMSLE=−0,0006,p=0,8331\Delta \text{RMSLE} = -0,0006, p = 0,8331) and small in classification (ΔPR-AUC=+0,0051\Delta \text{PR-AUC} = +0,0051).

Executive recommendations and action plan

Within the educational simulation, the report translates the statistical evidence and audited models into the following decisions for content and recommendation-engineering teams. Applying them to a real platform would require validation with observational data and an appropriate evaluation design.

Tactical decision matrix for creators and platforms

Factor / system Proposed action in the simulation Quantified impact in the dataset
Thumbnail design (thumbnail_face) Standardize expressive human faces in thumbnails across all editorial categories before upload. Mean increase of −0,8280→−0,6097-0,8280 \to -0,6097 in ln⁡(views/subs)\ln(\text{views}/\text{subs}) (+24,4%+24,4\% in views per subscriber) and an increase of 18,15%→22,78%18,15\% \to 22,78\% in the probability of reaching the top 20%.
Semantic indexing (tags_count) Fill in between 2020 and 3030 descriptive tags and maintain a balanced title-to-description ratio (tags_per_title_char). Second-largest individual TreeSHAP contributor (|SHAP|=0,0321|\text{SHAP}| = 0,0321) to the organic-reach multiplier (r=+0,0549,p=1,83×10−9r = +0,0549, p = 1,83 \times 10^{-9}).
Duration (duration_sec) and scheduling (upload_hour/day) Remove artificial duration cuts and publication-hour/day restrictions from the editorial calendar. Duration has no detected effect on views per subscriber (r=−0,0077,p=0,3966r = -0,0077, p = 0,3966), and hours/days show a null effect (p>0,31p > 0,31) in the experiment.
Channel benchmarking (confounding adjustment) Replace raw-view targets with the adjusted index M=ln⁡(views/subscriber_count)M = \ln(\text{views}/\text{subscriber\_count}), segmented by category. Avoids penalizing niche categories (Vlog, Travel) or falsely rewarding giant channels in high-turnover categories (Music, Comedy) within the simulation.

Recommendation-system deployment scenario (cold start) and study limitations

Architecture proposed for the simulated scenario (Cold Start Scoring)

  1. Inference at time zero (t = 0): Deploy the Ridge / LogisticRegression pair or LightGBM_DualRegressor, operating exclusively under Regime A (Cold Start) at video ingestion. Within this experiment, Regime A achieves PR-AUC = 0,7407 (LogisticRegression) and 0,7383 (LightGBM_DualRegressor), so waiting for post-upload engagement rates (Regime B, PR-AUC = 0,7409) offers little gain to justify the operational latency.
  2. Decision rule calibrated at quantile P80P_{80}: Use the calibrated threshold τ80\tau_{80} (p≥0,4028p \ge 0,4028 for the logistic classifier or ŷreg≥13,2225\hat{y}_{\text{reg}} \ge 13,2225 for the dual regressor) instead of the naive 0,500,50 cutoff. In the experiment, this choice raises F1-Score from 0,63970,6397 to 0,67010,6701, with precision of 67,08%67,08\% and recall of 66,94%66,94\% in the promotional-prioritization queue.
  3. Continuous contract guards (DC-01 to DC-07): Keep assert_no_leakage(X, regime="A") attached to the inference pipeline to prevent accidental introduction of raw interaction counts in future schema updates.

Methodological limitations and scope of generalization:

  • Synthetic, stationary dataset: The 12.00012.000 records come from a stationary parametric generator without external trend shocks, calendar seasonality or cross-video network effects. The report proposes evaluating view-growth velocity during the first two hours after upload (Δviews/Δt\Delta \text{views}/\Delta t) in real production data, monitored within strict time windows (Out-of-Time Validation); this experiment did not validate that additional signal.
  • Explanatory ceiling of tabular metadata without subscribers: As shown by the confounding-adjusted model in Task 3 (R² of 0,00460,0046 and RMSLE of 0,95000,9500 on ln⁡(views/subs)\ln(\text{views}/\text{subs})), superficial packaging metadata (thumbnail_face, tags_count, text lengths and category) capture statistically significant directional effects (p<10−30p < 10^{-30}) but leave much of the residual variance per subscriber unexplained. The report relates it to intrinsic audiovisual content quality and audience retention (watch time); because these variables are absent from this tabular schema, the experiment did not measure that explanation.
